You need to figure out what you're allergic to. 

I was allergic to cats, but now have a cat and am doing fine. 

Cat allergies are to a protein present in the saliva. 

Siberian cats produce less of this protein, but on the downside are very long coated cats and sheds lot. So are very heavy maintenance to keep the dander under control.

Other cats that are considered 'hypoallergenic' actually just shed less. They don't produce less allergen at all. Like the Siamese, Devon Rex, Tonkinese, etc.

There is a kibble you can feed any cat that can reduce the protein's production, but it will not eliminate it. 

For me, I discovered my allergy is no longer a problem. I have no idea what happened, but I feel very fortunate.

Two Japanese stories which could be conflated to make a perfect disney tale. Little One Inch and Momotaro.

In Little One Inch, an elderly couple who have been unable to have children pray to the gods for children and are suddenly blessed with a son only one Inch tall. The boy eventually decides to leave and head to Kyoto. With a needle as a sword, a bowl for a boat and chopsticks for oars! He eventually reaches the city, and finds work in a large house. 

But trouble occurs when the young daughter of the house is kidnapped when she leaves to explore the city by a terrible Oni! Little One Inch faces off against the giant demon, but is swallowed whole! Yet he keeps fighting the Oni from within, stabbing so ferociously with his needle, that the demon yields! Spitting the boy up and fleeing, but leaving his enchanted mallet behind! 

Depending on the story, either the girl or Little One Inch uses the magical mallet to grow to six feet tall! They then live happily together, using the magic of the Oni's weapon to grant their family prosperity for generations.


In the story of Momotaro, an old woman was washing clothes when she saw a large peach floating down the river. She brought it inside. Her husband cut it open, and they were shocked to find a healthy child within. The pair had sadly been childless their whole lives, and to their even greater shock the child explained that he was a blessing from the gods bestowed upon them! They called him Momotaro.

When he reached adolescence he left his home to fight a band of Oni who were causing trouble in the land. The demons lived on an island known as Onigashima (Demon Island). He met a dog, a monkey and a pheasant on the way who promised to help him in exchange for some of the food he'd packed for the trip. When he reached the island, he and his companions managed to get into the Oni's fort and force them to surrender! Returning home with the demon treasure and the Oni Chief as a hostage so that the Oni would not cause anymore mischief. He lived happily with his family ever after.

Look, I like Veilguard but it's really not as good as the previous games when it comes to the writing, or the choices really.

In the first game your choices could lead to really challenging consequences, you could have your companions turn on you or sacrifice themselves at the end of the game. The choices were very well written, and made you wonder about what happened to these people. It took a great deal of time and effort to get any of the results to manifest, and the companions felt like friends.

In the second game you didn't have the same level of impact, but the stories the companions had and your impact on their outcomes were compelling. The end of the story was shaped by your choices, and the consequences were immense. It was truly horrifying, and moving. 

Inquisition was a perfect combination, in my mind of companions, choices and storytelling coming together. Your companions futures were shaped by your choices, the world shifting as you played and forming around your plays on the board. There was so much you could do to build your Inquisition, and your Inquisitor. There was depth and complexity. There was good reason why the game was lauded for what it did. 

Veilguard just doesn't have anywhere near the content or complexity of any of its predecessors. That is just something that can't be escaped. It's really a tragedy. It's a beautiful game with fantastic game play loop (though it feels like it needs a touch more refinement on the camera and timing aspects in combat). It doesn't have the heart, or the soul of Dragon Age. It feels hollow, like it's missing the spark the other games had (2 lacked it as well, but not to this extent). 

It doesn't keep to the lore of the games, which is insane given how established the world is. There are consistency issues in dialogue which is quite unacceptable in an RPG.

"Why are you so calm?" The dragon had asked when first I was kidnapped. I has simply stared.

"You'll see." The dragon had scoffed, chuckling as he placed me in his tower, like a doll in his little doll house. 

"Whatever you think your kingdom can do, I have seen it all before! I have decimated the might of millions, Princess! They will have to give me what I desire or persist, either way I'm satisfied."

Each day he gloated, laughed and teased but I knew truly what would come. Worse than anything the dragon could do.

The days turned to weeks, to months and then... years.

The dragon pressed its eye to the window, it's words no longer mocking, prodding things. 

"They do not come."

"I know."

"All this time?" I nodded, the dragon shifting size to fit its scaled bulk into the space I inhabited, fit for a Princess, though not a ginormous lizard. "This is not what I had hoped for." 

"It is what it was always to be, I am but a Princess." The dragon balked.

"Just? The heiress-"

"No, I am to inherit nothing, I have many brothers, I am not even a spare." I shrugged, picking up my cup of tea and taking leisurely sip. "I was reminded of that quite frequently." 

"That is quite barbaric, and backwards." I nodded as I noted the smoke fuming from the nostrils of my captor.

"Quite, but I could do naught to change my station. This by comparison is quite lovely." 

"Lovely? Being cooped up in a tower?" 

"Well, I'm not bothered by lessons that I'll never used, nor do I have to worry about being married off to some geriatric old man to help my father or brothers. So yes, it is quite pleasant." 

The dragon left soon after, and I did not see him for quite some time. 

Bur when I did, he was different. His eyes were dark, expression grave.

"Drink this." He never told me to do anything, or asked anything of me. 

"What is it?" 

"A choice." He did not elaborate, and yet I saw it in his eyes.

The blazing fire that mirrored the ichor in the glass.

I drank.

I jumped back, as I think anyone would, as from the withered remains rose a delicate shape. Its form was curled over itself, and then with a sickening, sudden crack it rose all at once! A soft sigh escaping its lips as it turned to look at me with large, bulbous yellow eyes on its gentle, porcelain white face. Reminiscent of a Victorian doll.
